query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In these high‐entropy nanoparticles, the tendency to form short‐range chemical orders or localized elemental segregations—arising from specific interatomic interactions among the constituent metals—governs whether the initial single‐phase solid solution is maintained under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions (473–1923 K).
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios that are initially crystallized as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Expose the nanoparticles to high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions (473–1923 K) while varying the relative ratios of elements known to interact strongly (e.g., by modifying the Co/Mo ratio, as demonstrated in the supporting evidence).
generation.conditions: Test under controlled atmospheres (to avoid oxidation) and in relevant reaction environments (e.g., ammonia decomposition for catalysis and appropriate thermoelectric measurement setups) throughout the specified temperature range.
generation.structural_mediator: The extent and nature of short-range chemical ordering (or elemental segregation) that develops during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: Differential bonding interactions among the constituent metals lead to local ordering. When these interactions favor a uniform distribution, the solid solution remains stable; if they promote segregation, local phase separation ensues. This change in microstructure, particularly at the surface, can alter active sites and thus affect both catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that develop minimal short-range ordering (i.e., maintain uniform elemental distribution) will retain their structural integrity and display stable catalytic and thermoelectric behaviors, whereas those exhibiting pronounced local ordering or segregation will show degradation in these properties relative to their initial single-phase state.
generation.baseline: The initial single-phase, uniformly mixed HEA nanoparticles before high-temperature treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles with near-equal atomic ratios within the tested temperature range (473–1923 K) under controlled atmospheres; different compositions, environmental conditions, or larger particle sizes may involve additional or alternative stabilizing/destabilizing mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative influence of specific interatomic interactions on ordering and performance, as well as the potential role of other high-temperature phenomena (e.g., sintering or oxidation when atmospheres are not ideally controlled), remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize HEA nanoparticles with controlled, near-equal atomic ratios but deliberately vary the concentration of element pairs (e.g., adjusting the Co/Mo ratio) to modulate the propensity for short-range ordering. Expose all samples to catalytic (e.g., ammonia decomposition) and thermoelectric operating conditions over 473–1923 K and then characterize their phase structure and surface chemistry using high-resolution X-ray diffraction, TEM, and XPS, alongside measuring their catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (for phase and crystallinity changes)
Transmission electron microscopy (for local ordering and segregation)
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (for surface chemical composition)
Catalytic activity metrics (e.g., turnover frequency in ammonia decomposition)
Thermoelectric performance indicators (e.g., electrical conductivity, Seebeck coefficient)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If variations in the degree of short-range chemical ordering (or segregation) induced by changing elemental ratios do not correlate with corresponding changes in catalytic and thermoelectric performance relative to the unchanged initial single-phase, then the hypothesis that short-range ordering governs the operational stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Highly efficient decomposition of ammonia using high-entropy alloy catalysts

Abstract: Ammonia represents a promising liquid fuel for hydrogen storage, but its large-scale application is limited by the need for precious metal ruthenium (Ru) as catalyst. Here we report on highly efficient ammonia decomposition using novel high-entropy alloy (HEA) catalysts made of earth abundant elements. Quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles are synthesized in a single solid-solution phase with robust control over the Co/Mo atomic ratio, including those ratios considered to be immiscible according to the Co-Mo bimetallic phase diagram. These HEA nanoparticles demonstrate substantially enhanced catalytic activity and stability for ammonia decomposition, with improvement factors achieving >20 versus Ru catalysts. Catalytic activity of HEA nanoparticles is robustly tunable by varying the Co/Mo ratio, allowing for the optimization of surface property to maximize the reactivity under different reaction conditions.
